subtype: Approach: revising the story after repeated no's [Revision]
passage:
Urmila: Fifteen replies, and the same line in every one. "Come back when there are customers."
Ritu: I know. I've read them again and again.
Urmila: So what are they telling us?
Ritu: That the deck isn't the problem. I've been fixing slides when I should have been finding customers.
Urmila: Then no more pitching until that changes.
Ritu: Agreed. I'll call the three clinics that tried the demo and ask if they'd sign a pilot.
Urmila: And if one says no?
Ritu: Then I ask what would make it a yes.
A month later, in the same room:
Ritu: Three pilots signed. Ready to send the new deck.
Urmila: Send it to the ones who wrote "customers".

qa.q: How many pilots did Ritu sign?
What was Ritu feeling while reading the fifteen replies again?
qa.a: Ritu felt frustrated and a bit ashamed of polishing slides instead of the real gap, as the admission about fixing slides shows.

qa.q: What could Ritu ask a clinic that says no to a pilot?
qa.a: Ritu could ask what would need to change for a yes, which gives evidence about the gap.

qa.q: How might an investor who wrote "Come back when there are customers" see the new deck?
qa.a: That investor would see someone who listened and came back with evidence that answers the concern.

grounding: The dialogue shows a founder who stops pitching after repeated identical rejections, signs pilot customers to fill the gap and returns with better evidence.
